summary: Updates and corrects the IANA XML Security URIs registry, which lists URIs for algorithms and information types used with XML signatures, encryption, canonicalization, and key management. It also fixes three errata against RFC 6931 and obsoletes it.

eli5.summary: A list of names for XML security tools is cleaned up and corrected.

questions: how are new xml security uris registered
subtitle: A corrected, updated list of the URIs that name algorithms and key types in XML signatures and encryption.

tldr.problem: XML signatures and XML encryption identify every algorithm and key information type by a URI, and the list of such URIs had grown across several documents and contained errors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9231 gathers the URIs in one reference, adds new ones (such as ChaCha20, Poly1305, EdDSA, X25519, HKDF and the XMSS signatures) under a new W3C prefix, fixes three errata, and updates the IANA 'XML Security URIs' registry to match.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6931 and is the current reference for the registry. Listing a URI is not an endorsement of the algorithm behind it.

today: RFC 9231 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6931, and the metadata lists no later RFC replacing it. It is the reference for the IANA XML Security URIs registry.

sections.title: Why XML Security Needs a URI List
sections.content:
XML digital signatures, canonicalization and encryption were standardized by the W3C and by the joint IETF/W3C XMLDSIG working group. These documents use URIs to identify algorithms and keying information types. RFC 9231 is a convenient reference list of those URIs and the algorithms they stand for.

It updates the IANA XML Security URIs registry, fixes three errata (Err3597, Err3965 and Err4004) and obsoletes RFC 6931. It is not a protocol specification and says it is not meant to change any algorithm implementation requirements of IETF or W3C documents.

Listing a URI does not endorse the algorithm for any purpose. The document simply supplies the URIs and the formatting used with them.
sections.eli5: Every tool in the XML security toolbox needs a name that every program agrees on. This document is the list of those names.

sections.title: URI Prefixes and Where New Names Live
sections.content:
Algorithm URIs share a few common prefixes. Original XML Signature URIs start with http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#. Algorithms added by RFC 4051 start with http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more#, those added by RFC 6931 with http://www.w3.org/2007/05/xmldsig-more#, and those added by this document with http://www.w3.org/2021/04/xmldsig-more#.

The W3C froze the first three prefixes: 2000/09/xmldsig# is frozen by the W3C, 2001/04/xmldsig-more# was frozen with RFC 4051 and 2007/05/xmldsig-more# was frozen with RFC 6931. Further URIs under them are prohibited. The W3C assigned the 2021 prefix for new URIs in this document.

An xmldsig-more URI implies no official W3C or IETF status for the algorithm. Dereferencing such a URI may or may not return a placeholder document.
sections.eli5: Names are grouped by the year they were handed out, like numbered coat hooks. Old hooks are full and locked, so new names go on a new hook.

sections.title: Algorithm Families Covered
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC groups the algorithms by the XML element that uses them. DigestMethod hashes include MD5, SHA-224, SHA-384, Whirlpool and the SHA-3 family. SignatureMethod covers MAC algorithms (HMAC variants, Poly1305, SipHash-2-4) and public key signatures (RSA, ECDSA, ESIGN, RSASSA-PSS and Edwards-curve signatures).

Other groups are Minimal Canonicalization, Transform algorithms (XPointer), EncryptionMethod algorithms (ARCFOUR, Camellia, key encapsulation mechanisms, SEED, ChaCha20 and ChaCha20+Poly1305), key agreement (X25519 and X448) and key derivation (HKDF).

Each entry gives an identifier, a short description and usually an example element. For digests, the DigestValue content is the base64 encoding of the digest bytes. For instance, a SHA-224 digest is a 224-bit string sent as a 28-octet stream. Where text is duplicated from RFC 3275, that RFC is normative in case of conflict.
sections.eli5: The list is sorted by job: some names are for shrinking data to a fingerprint, some for signing, some for locking, and some for agreeing on a secret key.

sections.title: New Algorithms Added Here
sections.content:
Appendix A lists what this RFC adds over RFC 6931: Poly1305 (2.2.4), SipHash-2-4 (2.2.5), XMSS and XMSSMT (2.2.6), ECDSA with SHA3 (2.3.6), Edwards-curve signatures (2.3.12), ChaCha20 (2.6.7), ChaCha20+Poly1305 (2.6.8), X25519 (2.7.1) and HKDF (2.8.1).

Some details the text gives: Poly1305 takes a 32-octet one-time key and yields a 16-octet tag. SipHash computes a 64-bit MAC from a 128-bit secret key. Ed25519 uses 32-octet public keys and 64-octet signatures, while Ed448 uses 57-octet public keys and 114-octet signatures. ChaCha20 takes a 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce and a 32-bit counter.

XMSS and XMSSMT are stateful hash-based signature schemes. The text says the careful state management they need is described in NIST SP 800-208. HKDF inputs are mapped onto XML child elements of AgreementMethod such as Salt, OriginatorKeyInfo, KA-Nonce and KeySize.
sections.eli5: New tools got new name tags, such as a fast scrambler called ChaCha20 and new signature stamps. Each tag also says how big its keys and results are.

sections.title: KeyInfo Types and the Two Indexes
sections.content:
Section 3 adds a PKCS7signedData child element for KeyInfo, which can carry a base64-encoded PKCS #7 bag of certificates and CRLs (any signer information is ignored). It also lists extra Type values for RetrievalMethod, such as rawPGPKeyPacket and rawX509CRL. Raw types need a Type attribute because they are not unambiguously parsable.

Section 4 provides two indexes of every URI, one by fragment (the part after the hash sign) and one by full URI. Each row points to the section of this RFC, or the standard, that specifies the item.
sections.eli5: There are also name tags for kinds of keys and certificates, plus two lookup tables: one sorted by short name and one by full address.

sections.title: Corrections to RFC 6931
sections.content:
Appendix B names two bad URIs that RFC 6931 contained. 2006/12/xmlc12n11# should have been 2006/12/xmlc14n11# (Err3965), and 2007/05/xmldsig-more#rsa-sha224 should have been 2001/04/xmldsig-more#rsa-sha224 (Err4004).

Both stay in the indexes, marked {Bad}. The rule is that implementations SHOULD only generate the correct URI but SHOULD understand both the correct and the erroneous one. Other changes were new XML examples, updated references and editorial fixes.
sections.eli5: Two names in the old list had typos. The new list keeps the typos recognized so old messages still work, but tells everyone to write the right name from now on.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA has established a registry called XML Security URIs and updated it to match Section 4.2, with references to this RFC. New entries are added by Specification Required, judged by a designated expert.

The criteria are documentation sufficient for interoperability of the algorithm or data type and its XML syntax, and sufficient importance, normally shown by inclusion in an approved W3C Note, Proposed Recommendation or Recommendation, or in an approved RFC.
sections.eli5: A librarian keeps the official list. To add a new name, you must show a written description that lets others use it, and that it matters enough to be in an official document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC only documents URIs, so the security considerations vary with each algorithm. General XML security considerations are outside its scope. Readers are pointed to RFC 6151 before using MD5 as a digest or HMAC-MD5 or RSA-MD5 as a signature method, and to RFC 6194 for SHA-1.

The text also warns that algorithms weaken over time, so implementations should be modular and ready for the set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms to change. This is called algorithm agility.
sections.eli5: Locks get easier to pick as time passes, so build your system so you can swap in a better lock later.
